title: What’s still broken or unreliable when using AI agents for trading?
author: No_Progress92
selftext:
I’ve been experimenting with AI agents for market research, signal generation, and some workflow automation around trading.

They help with speed and coverage, but some parts still feel fragile or unreliable in practice.

Curious what others are running into:

* What’s one thing AI agents still get wrong more often than they should in trading workflows?
* Where do they break most often (signal quality, execution logic, data handling, risk checks, etc.)?
* Have you found any practical workarounds that actually help?

Looking for real experiences, not just success stories.

comments.author: Slight_Ad_6375
comments.body:
\- I like that they know pretty much all the option math that I need and how to apply them.   
\- It writes a lot of code very fast. But somehow it forgets what it wrote itself, because its memory files are too bloated.  
\- I do not like that they are not very imaginative  
\- Their financial advise is as good as Jim Cramer's  
\- Claude Opus 5 talks like an alien from New York. 

Other than its voice, I don't think it can independently make decisions and money yet.

However, its option math and coding powers allowed me to more than double my premium yield.

replies.author: No_Progress92
replies.body:
This matches a lot of what I’ve seen too.

The option math and coding speed are clearly strong. The weak parts are memory/context management, limited creativity, and the fact that the financial judgment still isn’t reliable enough to trust independently.

Interesting that even with those limits, the coding + options knowledge was still enough to more than double premium yield. That seems like the current sweet spot — using it as a high-speed assistant rather than an autonomous decision-maker.

replies.author: Slight_Ad_6375
replies.body: For me, I don't have deep quant background, but I have ideas that I can articulate in english. Its pretty cool that claude could find a well established academic paper that has the math, plus prior pros and cons about the idea, and then quickly test it out for me.

replies.author: No_Progress92
replies.body:
That’s a really good use case.

Having the idea in plain English and then letting the model pull the relevant paper, surface the math, and quickly test it is honestly one of the stronger workflows right now — especially if you don’t come from a deep quant background.

The research + rapid prototyping loop seems more reliable than asking it to independently make trading decisions.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: The memory bloat issue is real and it's the thing that kills most agent setups. They write code fine but then forget their own context because the files are a mess. Fix that by keeping separate, lean memory files per strategy instead of one giant blob. And yeah, the financial judgment is still Jim Cramer-tier  -  use agents for research and option math, never for the final call. The workaround that actually works is what someone mentioned: describe your idea in plain English, let the model find the academic paper and test it. That loop is reliable. Anything beyond that is gambling with extra steps.
